rows.text: ## Why this one first The inbox was the only place where volume and a measurable outcome met. Every other candidate needed a survey to tell whether it had worked, and a metric you have to ask about is a metric you cannot gate a release on. ## What made it shippable Three things, in this order. An eval set built from tickets that had already been answered, so there was a known-good answer to compare against. Tracing on every call, so a bad answer could be traced to the retrieval step rather than argued about. A cost ceiling per ticket, checked in the same CI job as the evals. ## What I built, in order | Part | What it's for | | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Eval set from real tickets | A known-good answer to check every change against, before it reaches a customer. | | [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) as the tool boundary | Keeps what the agent is allowed to call explicit and narrow, instead of improvised inside a prompt. | | [OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io) tracing | Every call recorded, so a wrong answer traces back to a retrieval step, not a guess. | | GitHub Actions eval gate | Runs the eval set on every change so a regression blocks the merge before it reaches a ticket. | ## What I would do differently I built the first eval set from tickets that had already been answered well. Seasonality made the first week of results look better than the system was. Sampling across a longer window would have caught that before anyone celebrated.

rows.text: The distinction that matters is between a single prompt and response and a task an agent sees through to the end. A chatbot that answers one question is not agentic. A system that reads a support ticket, looks up the order, drafts a refund and issues it, is agentic: nobody scripted that exact sequence in advance. Engineering teams build this pattern because it automates the cross-system judgement calls that used to need a person. Security reviewers and boards ask about it separately from the model itself, because the risk changes once a system can act, not only speak. A wrong sentence in a chat reply is embarrassing. A wrong action against a live order or a payment has already happened by the time anyone notices, because nothing stood between the decision and the outcome.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up It comes up the moment a pitch or a product description says "agent" instead of "assistant". A security reviewer's next question is almost always what the agent can do without asking first, since that is where the real exposure sits, not the model choice. A board hears "agentic" and correctly hears "this thing takes actions on its own." That is a different risk conversation than a chatbot that only produces text. ## What to do about it List every action an agent can take, not just what it can say, and sign off on each as a separate risk. Set a real limit on what it can do without a person confirming first, especially anything that spends money, touches a customer record, or sends something external. Log every tool call, so a bad outcome traces to a specific decision. Evals belong here: test the whole action chain, not just the model's replies.

rows.text: AI governance is the accountability layer above an AI system - who is allowed to build or buy it, and who answers, by name, when it fails. It runs through the policies, roles and controls that decide what data a system may touch and who signs off before it reaches customers.
rows.reason: head.title/body.h1 checked against docs/SEMANTIC-CORE.md's generated per-family grammar (exact match or explained by documented ungated-utility-route/stale-cache exception); body.p composed strings (excerpts, tag/category joins, dated metadata lines) read as coherent whole sentences with no truncation, duplication, or missing-space artifacts against the built site/dist page.

rows.text: AI governance sits above the technology itself. It covers who owns each AI system, what data it may touch, which use cases are off limits, and who signs off before a system reaches customers. That shows up as a register of the systems in use, a policy engineers actually follow, and a review step before anything new goes live. A customer's procurement team asks for it during a security review. A board asks after a pilot nears production, once someone raises who is liable for a bad call. Regulators ask for pieces of it too, through frameworks like the NIST AI RMF and standards like ISO/IEC 42001. In practice, it changes three things. Someone specific owns each AI system, instead of it belonging to whichever team built it. A new system needs sign-off before it touches customer data. A written answer exists the day a customer or auditor asks for one.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up An insurer asks who owns AI risk before writing a policy. A board member reads about an AI failure elsewhere and asks what would happen here. An investor's due-diligence checklist now has a line for it too. Write down who is responsible for each system, and who would notice if it started producing worse answers. ## What to do about it Start with a one-page register: every AI system in use, who owns it, what data it touches, and whether customer data leaves the building. Assign one named owner per system, not a team. Add a single sign-off step before a new system reaches production. Map what you already do against the NIST AI RMF or ISO/IEC 42001, not to get certified immediately, but so you have a recognised structure to point at.

rows.text: The EU AI Act calls this a fundamental rights impact assessment. Article 27 requires it from deployers that are public-law bodies or private entities delivering a public service. It also applies to any deployer using a high-risk system to score creditworthiness. The same goes for pricing life and health insurance. The assessment has to name the process the system sits inside, how often it runs, and which people or groups it is likely to affect. It has to describe the human oversight in place, and the governance and complaint routes that kick in if a risk shows up. The deployer sends the finished assessment to the national market surveillance authority. Article 27 lets this assessment build on an existing data protection impact assessment rather than repeat it. Where the two overlap, the newer document only has to add what the DPIA does not already answer.

rows.text: That cycle is what the standard specifies in full, covering policy, risk treatment, resourcing and internal audit for the whole organisation rather than one product. Building to this shape does not require certifying against it. A management system is a way of working; certification is a separate, optional proof of it. The EU AI Act does not require this broader system. Article 17 requires a narrower relative of it instead. Every provider of a high-risk AI system must run a documented quality management system, covering the risk-management process, post-market monitoring and serious-incident procedures among other elements. Its depth scales to the size of the provider's organisation. That overlap is why the two get treated as one project, not two. Building the policy, the register and the review cycle once tends to satisfy the voluntary standard. For a provider of high-risk systems, it also tends to satisfy the legal minimum Article 17 sets.

rows.text: For almost every high-risk system, the outcome is simple: the provider checks its own work against the rules and signs a declaration, with no outside reviewer involved. Only biometric-identification systems sometimes need an independent outside checker, a "notified body," to sign off instead. Article 43 sets this split by Annex III area, the EU AI Act's list of high-risk use cases. Every area except biometric identification uses Annex VI, the self-check route with no notified body involved. Biometric identification uses Annex VII's notified-body route wherever harmonised standards, the detailed technical rules the Commission recognises as proof of compliance, are not fully applied or do not yet exist. The one exception is a system that keeps learning after deployment. A provider can plan for that drift in advance and record it in the technical documentation before the first assessment. rows.text: A DPIA, short for data protection impact assessment, is a written GDPR review completed before a company begins personal-data processing likely to carry high privacy risk. It assesses what data is collected, why, and how that risk is being reduced, distinct from a fairness review of the decision itself.

rows.text: GDPR Article 35 makes this review mandatory, not a judgement call, in three situations. One is large-scale profiling with legal or similarly significant effects. Another is large-scale processing of special-category data, such as health or biometric records. The third is systematic large-scale monitoring of a public space. Most consequential AI systems land in the first of these by default. It has to describe the processing and why it is necessary. It has to assess the risk to the people concerned and set out the measures that reduce it. Where the company has appointed a data protection officer, that officer must be consulted while the assessment is carried out. Signing off afterward does not count. Where the system is high-risk under the EU AI Act, Article 26 points the other way too. A deployer must draw on the information the provider supplies under Article 13 when carrying out this GDPR assessment. The two obligations end up sharing evidence, not separate files.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up Almost any AI system worth building processes personal data, which makes a DPIA the default question rather than an edge case. Legal or procurement asks for it specifically once a system moves from a prototype to something touching real customer records. Start from what is actually being collected and why, not from a template's headings, and consult the data protection officer while there is time to act. rows.text: Formally Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Act entered into force on 1 August 2024. It sorts AI systems into a risk ladder, from banned practices, to a high-risk category, to a lighter set of transparency duties. High-risk covers things like hiring, credit and law enforcement. The lighter duties apply to systems such as chatbots. Everything else is left largely unregulated. Obligations scale with the tier. High-risk systems carry duties such as a conformity assessment, technical documentation, human oversight, and registration in an EU database. The Act applies to any company whose AI system is used in the EU, not only companies based there. That is why a US-based startup with European customers cannot treat this as someone else's problem. In practice, it changes what "we did not think about that" costs. For a high-risk use case, a company now needs a documented risk assessment and a named point of human oversight, with evidence of both ready before a regulator or a customer's legal team asks.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up It comes up the moment a company has, or wants, a customer in the EU, regardless of where it is based. A customer's legal team asks which risk tier your product falls into before they sign, because their own exposure depends on your answer. A board asks about it once a competitor gets fined, or a customer raises it at renewal. The Act follows the AI system's users, not the provider's registered address. ## What to do about it Work out which risk tier each AI system falls into. Most products used inside a normal business are not high-risk, but a few categories, hiring and credit among them, almost always are and deserve a real legal read. For anything near the high-risk category, start the paperwork now: a risk assessment, a named oversight point, and technical documentation. For everything else, keep the register entry current, so the answer is a lookup, not a scramble.

rows.text: The comparison that matters is to an ordinary test suite. There is one difference: the system under test can give a different answer each run. A typical eval is a set of inputs with known good answers or a scoring rule. It runs automatically whenever the prompt, the model or the surrounding code changes, with a pass rate tracked over time rather than a single pass or fail. rows.text: In practice a guardrail is one of three things: a topic restriction on what the model will engage with, or an output filter on what a user sees. rows.text: A high-risk AI system is one the EU AI Act classifies as carrying its heaviest legal duties. That happens either because it is a safety component of a regulated product, or because it serves a listed purpose such as hiring, credit scoring or law enforcement. A narrow exemption can apply.
rows.reason: head.title/body.h1 checked against docs/SEMANTIC-CORE.md's generated per-family grammar (exact match or explained by documented ungated-utility-route/stale-cache exception); body.p composed strings (excerpts, tag/category joins, dated metadata lines) read as coherent whole sentences with no truncation, duplication, or missing-space artifacts against the built site/dist page.

rows.text: A system reaches the category one of two ways. Article 6(1) covers the first: a safety component of, or itself, a product already regulated under EU product-safety law, such as medical devices or machinery. That underlying law already requires third-party conformity assessment. Annex III covers the second: eight listed use-case areas, among them biometric identification, employment decisions, credit scoring and law enforcement. Article 6(2) makes a system high-risk for landing in one of those areas alone, with no product-safety law involved at all. A system inside Annex III can still escape the label under Article 6(3), for four narrow reasons. One is a limited procedural task: reformatting an application into a standard template, say. Another is improving a human decision already made, such as tidying a report's wording without changing its recommendation. A third is detecting a deviation without replacing human judgement, such as flagging an unusual transaction for a fraud analyst to review. The fourth is a preparatory task ahead of someone else's assessment, such as gathering a loan applicant's documents before a human underwriter looks at them. None of the four survives contact with profiling: a system that profiles individual people is high-risk regardless.

rows.text: The concept sits on a spectrum, from full autonomy at one end to human-on-the-loop at the other, where a person can intervene but does not have to act. Human-in-the-loop sits in between: a person must actively approve each step before it happens. Where a system falls on that spectrum is a design decision, not a fixed property of the technology. It is one of the first things a customer's security team or a regulator asks about, for anything that can affect a person's money, employment or legal standing. Article 14 of the EU AI Act requires "effective" human oversight for high-risk systems: oversight that can genuinely catch and correct a bad output, not a person who clicks approve without reading it. In practice, this decides where a company can safely remove a person from a workflow, and where it still needs one.

rows.text: Article 14 splits the mechanism into two kinds of measure. Some are built into the system itself by the provider before it ships. An example is an interface that flags a low-confidence output. Others are measures the provider identifies for the deployer to carry out instead, such as a rule about when a person must review a case before it proceeds. Article 14 spells out five specific capacities the overseeing person needs. They must understand the system's real limits well enough to spot a malfunction, and stay alert to automation bias rather than trusting the output by default. They also need to correctly read what the output actually means, disregard or reverse a specific output when needed, and have a way to halt the system outright.

An auditor tests this by asking what the overseer would do in a specific bad case, not whether a review step exists on a diagram. ## What to do about it Name the specific person or role authorised to halt each high-risk system, not a team, and check they have time per case to evaluate output rather than approve on reflex. Train that person specifically on automation bias. A rushed or over-trusting reviewer defeats the requirement even when the process looks correct. rows.text: ISO/IEC's joint technical committee for artificial intelligence published it in December 2023. It specifies requirements for an AI management system: the recurring policies, roles and processes that govern how an organisation develops, provides or uses AI. It uses the same Plan-Do-Check-Act structure as other ISO management-system standards, such as ISO/IEC 27001 for information security. Unlike the NIST AI RMF, a free framework, ISO/IEC 42001 is a standard a company can be audited and certified against by an accredited third party. Enterprise customers and procurement teams ask for it, or ask where you sit against it, because certification gives them a documented, externally checked answer instead of a vendor's own claim. In practice, working towards it means three things: writing down a risk-assessment method, running an inventory of AI systems, and reviewing that inventory on a schedule. rows.text: Every call to any model passes through one place, instead of going straight from application code to a vendor's API. Through that point, a company can control who is allowed to call a model. It can log every prompt and response for an audit trail, and redact sensitive data before it leaves the building. Without a gateway, API keys end up scattered across a codebase, and nobody holds a full log of what was sent to a vendor. A data leak through a prompt stays invisible until a customer or regulator finds it first. Engineering teams adopt one to stop rebuilding the same authentication and logging code in every project that touches a model. It also gives a direct, specific answer to a vendor questionnaire's question about how model access is controlled. That beats a description of several applications each doing it inconsistently.

rows.text: Most companies between 30 and 300 people already have staff using AI tools, whether or not a policy says so. The policy that works is not the longest one. It states which data may go where, who approves a new tool, and what happens when someone gets it wrong, in language a new hire reads in one sitting. ## What does a working AI acceptable use policy actually need to say? A policy that survives contact with real staff decides a short list of things, not a long one. Six sections make up a working one. Each row here names the section, the decision it forces, and the specific failure it exists to prevent. | Section | What it decides | Failure it prevents | | --------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Scope | Which staff, contractors and AI tools the policy covers. | A contractor or a new hire assuming the rules do not apply to them. | | Data classification | Which data tier may reach which category of AI vendor. | Client or personal data pasted into a public chatbot with no data agreement. | | Approved tools and requests | Which AI systems are pre-approved, and how staff add another one. | Staff picking an unapproved tool because asking takes too long. | | Human review | Whether a person checks AI output before it reaches a customer, a contract or a filing. | An unreviewed AI draft going out under someone's name. | | Customer disclosure | When a customer must be told they are talking to an AI system or seeing AI-made content. | A hidden AI interaction reaching a customer where disclosure is a legal duty. | | Vendor training use | Whether a vendor may use company or client input to train its own models. | Confidential input quietly improving a vendor's public model. | | Ownership and review | Who owns the policy, and how often it is checked against what staff actually use. | A policy that describes a tool nobody uses, and stays silent about the one everyone does. | | Incident reporting | What staff do the moment an AI system produces something wrong or exposes data. | A bad output or a leak going unreported because nobody knew who to tell. | | Enforcement | What happens after a breach, and who decides. | A rule everyone knows is never actually enforced. | The customer disclosure row is not optional once a system talks to people outside the company. Article 50 of the EU AI Act already requires a provider or a deployer to tell a person they are interacting with an AI system. It also requires labelling content the system generated, whether or not that system counts as high-risk. A staff-facing policy has to name who checks that duty before a customer-facing AI feature ships, not leave it to whoever built the feature to remember. ## What should the policy refuse to try to do? A policy that tries to be the technical control fails twice. It fails once because a paragraph of text cannot stop a paste into a browser, and again because staff read that overreach as proof the whole document is for show. Access limits, contract terms and vendor settings do the technical work. The policy states the rule those controls exist to support. Listing every approved tool by name reads as complete on the day it is published. It is wrong within weeks, because a new model or a new vendor account always arrives faster than a document gets updated. A policy built around named tools also implies that anything missing from the list is quietly fine, which is the opposite of what a reviewer wants to see. An outright ban is the easiest policy to write and the least effective one to run. It does not remove the reason someone went looking for an AI tool in the first place. It just moves that search out of sight, where it is much harder to see or govern. ## What do you do about the tools staff are already using? By the time a policy is drafted, some staff are already using AI without asking anyone first. That means drafting client emails in a personal chatbot account, running a browser extension nobody vetted, or building a habit around a coding assistant they picked themselves. That is [shadow AI](/glossary/shadow-ai), and treating it as rare is the first mistake a policy can make. Two moves fix more of it than a warning email does. First, make the approved path faster than the workaround: a fast yes for a low-risk tool beats a slow review nobody wants to wait for. Second, check instead of asking. Checking browser extensions, expense claims and what the company actually pays AI vendors shows what people are really running, which beats trusting a self-reported survey. ## What happens when someone breaks the policy? Most breaches are not sabotage. Someone pastes a client's contract into a personal chatbot account to move faster, not to leak it. That is different from someone who was told a tool was blocked and used it anyway, or who hid AI involvement in work they signed off as their own. A policy that cannot tell the two apart will punish the wrong case or excuse the real one. One named role decides what happens next: the same person who owns the AI register and the policy itself, not a group chat and not a vote. They classify what happened, decide whether legal or an affected client needs to hear about it, and choose the response, from a conversation to removal of access to company systems. That decision runs through the disciplinary process HR already has for any other policy breach. The AI policy does not need a punishment system of its own; it needs a clear point where that existing process starts. Silence is its own answer too: a policy that never states what happens after a breach gets tested once, and staff learn from the result whether any of it is real. ## Who should own it, and how does it stay current? The same person who is already accountable for AI risk generally should hold this document. A shared inbox cannot hold it, because someone has to be answerable when a customer or an auditor asks a direct question. [ISO/IEC 42001](/glossary/iso-iec-42001) treats a policy like this as one part of a management system, reviewed on a schedule and checked against a live inventory. A review interval only works if it is tied to something that actually changes: a new hire, a new vendor account, a client contract that names a data rule of its own. Quarterly is a reasonable default for a company this size. The exact interval matters less than the fact that one exists and someone is accountable for keeping it. The version I run for my own practice is public at [my AI policy](/ai-policy), one page, as a worked example of the same shape at a much smaller scale. The [Starter Kit](/resources/ai-governance-starter-kit) sets out the same structure as a table you can copy, sized for a company with more than one person to coordinate. ## What doesn't a policy like this solve? A written policy does not tell you whether anyone inside the company actually owns AI risk today. If nobody does, that gap usually surfaces during an [AI readiness and risk assessment](/services/ai-readiness-and-risk-assessment) before it ever reaches the policy stage, because there is no obvious person to hand the draft to. Someone determined to break the rule will do it regardless; no policy stops that. What it removes is the excuse of not knowing, and it gives the company a fair, defensible reason to act when someone crosses the line anyway. Nobody enforces it without an owner, a review date and a stated consequence. Skip those and it is a page people skim once and never open again.

A regression gets caught before a reviewer approves the pull request, not after a customer notices. Build the set from real production traffic. rows.text: An eval suite that only runs on a laptop protects nobody. The same regression a developer catches by eye on a good day slips through on a bad one, and a model provider's silent update slips through every time. Putting [an eval suite](/glossary/evals) in CI turns a habit into a gate. The pull request cannot merge until the numbers clear, whoever is watching. ## How do you build an eval set from production traffic? Pull the first cases from what the agent has actually handled, not from what a spec said it should handle. Real traces carry the phrasing, the edge cases, and the odd multi-step requests. A person writing test data from imagination never thinks to include them. A support agent's eval set should read like a week of its own transcripts, because that is exactly what it is. Sample across a period long enough that one good or bad week does not decide the result. On only.help, my own product, the support-triage rollout built its first eval set from tickets already answered. It then found that the [first week looked better than the system really was](/case-studies/only-help-agentic-support), purely from seasonal timing. A month of traffic spans weekdays, weekends, and spikes the business already expects, which is a sturdier base than one convenient week. Mix the set on purpose. Include three kinds of case: routine ones that should always pass, a handful known to be hard, and a few with no single acceptable answer. Most agent tasks in production fall into that last kind. Store the set next to the code that it tests, in a format a reviewer can read in a pull request, and change it through the same review a code change gets. Revisit the set on a fixed schedule rather than whenever someone remembers. Retire a case once the product has genuinely outgrown it. Add one the day a new failure reaches production. That keeps the set tracking how the agent is actually used. ## How do you score an agent when there is no golden answer? Most agent tasks do not reduce to one correct string, so do not force them into that shape. A support reply, a summary, or a multi-step tool sequence can be right in more than one way. A scorer built for exact match will reject good answers as often as it catches bad ones. Score in layers instead, cheapest and most reliable checks first. Start with deterministic checks on anything mechanical. Check whether the agent called the right tool, with a valid argument set, in a shape that downstream code can actually parse. These checks are cheap, and they never disagree with themselves. In most agentic systems, they catch a large share of regressions before a judge ever runs. OWASP's list of risks in large language model applications names excessive agency as one of the standard failure modes worth testing for. Excessive agency means an agent taking an action its task never asked for. Write a case for every tool the agent can call. Each case should check that the tool stays quiet when not needed, and that it fires correctly when needed. For the answer's content, add a reference-free judge. Look at the question and whatever the agent actually retrieved. Then check whether every claim in the answer traces back to a document it had in hand. This catches a fluent, confident answer that is not supported by anything the system looked at, which is the failure mode a plain accuracy score misses entirely. Where no rubric fits cleanly, fall back to a comparison against the last known-good version. Show a judge both outputs, blind to which one is new, and ask it to pick a winner. A judge finds picking a winner easier than defending an absolute score out of some invented scale. A win rate against a fixed baseline is also a steadier number to watch than a score with no anchor. NIST's AI RMF frames this as a selection problem under its Measure function. Which method fits depends on what is actually being measured. A team documents why it chose a metric, and which ones it rejected. That team ends up with a sturdier suite than one that picked whatever was easiest to compute. ## What happens when the judge itself is flaky? A judge model can score the same input differently on two runs, especially at a higher temperature. That alone will make a pipeline look unstable, even when the agent under test has not changed. Set the judge's own temperature as low as the provider allows. Treat any remaining run-to-run disagreement as a property of the judge to manage. Calibrate the judge on a fixed schedule against a small set of cases a human has already scored. The number that matters is agreement between the judge and the human reviewers. A judge that is consistent but consistently wrong is worse than one that is honestly uncertain. Consistent wrongness hides the problem instead of surfacing it. Let the judge decline a case it cannot confidently assess. A skipped case should fall out of the pass-rate calculation, rather than count as either a pass or a fail. A case the judge skips often is telling you the rubric does not cover that situation yet. When one specific case flips between pass and fail on identical re-runs, treat that case as broken, not the whole gate. Quarantine it. Keep it running so you can see it, stop it from blocking a merge, and put a name against fixing its rubric or its sampling. Only then should it rejoin the set that actually gates a build. ## What should the pipeline check, and what does a failing check do to the build? Not every check should carry the same weight. A wrong tool call and a slow response are both real problems, but only one of them should stop a release. The table below is the shape of a working gate. It shows what each row measures, how it gets a number, and what that number does to the build when it fails. | What to score | How to score it | What a failing score does to the build | | ---------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Task success on labelled cases | Exact match or a deterministic rule against a known-good answer. | Blocks the merge immediately, with no override. | | Task success with no golden answer | A rubric-based judge scores the answer against stated criteria, not against a reference. | Blocks the merge once the pass rate drops below the floor set for that task. | | Faithfulness to retrieved context | A reference-free judge checks whether each claim traces back to a document the agent actually retrieved. | Blocks the merge; an unsupported claim counts as a defect, not a style note. | | Preference against the last good version | Pairwise comparison: the judge sees both outputs, blind to which is new, and picks a winner. | Blocks the merge if the new version loses on more cases than the agreed margin allows. | | Tool-call correctness | Deterministic check that the agent called the right tool with a valid, schema-checked argument set. | Blocks the merge; a malformed call fails loudly instead of degrading quietly. | | Judge-human agreement | Re-run the rubric against a human-labelled sample on a fixed schedule and compare agreement. | Does not block a single pull request; a drop pages the eval owner to fix the rubric. | | Cost per completed run | Sum of model and tool cost across the eval set, divided by cases completed. | Blocks the merge once the run exceeds the ceiling set in the pipeline config. | | Response time under load | Wall-clock time per case, measured in the same job as the scores. | Warns on the pull request; blocks only if it breaches the budget agreed with the product owner. | ## Where does the cost ceiling sit? Put a cost ceiling in the same job as the quality score. Do not put it on a separate dashboard someone checks once a week. Agent systems fail commercially long before they fail technically. Consider a tool call that retries a few times on a bad response: harmless in a demo, ruinous once real traffic hits it. Measure cost per completed run, across the whole eval set, the way you measure the pass rate. A change that makes the agent slower or more expensive without a real gain is a regression, even if every other score stays green. A [90-Day Production Sprint](/services/90-day-production-sprint) puts this gate in place before a workflow takes its first real user. That is a cheaper time to find the problem than after the first invoice. ## What does the pipeline do when a check fails? A failing check blocks the merge by default. The pull request gets a summary next to the diff that caused it. That summary lists which cases failed, what the agent returned, and what the check expected. Nobody reconstructs the failure from a log. Not every failure deserves the same response. A wrong tool call or an unsupported claim should stop the release outright. A latency or cost warning close to its budget, or a drop in judge-human agreement, can page an owner instead, without stopping every other change in the queue. Keep that distinction explicit in the pipeline config, not in someone's memory of which checks are actually load-bearing. Only a named reviewer, not the author of the change, can override a hard block. That override has to write itself into the same log the eval results live in. An override that leaves no trace is indistinguishable from no gate at all. It gets used that way the next time someone is in a hurry.

rows.text: A security review of an AI system usually starts with one question: what is actually running. If the honest answer takes a week of digging through chat logs and old tickets, the review stalls before it reaches architecture or data flows. An AI system register is the fix: one document listing every AI system a company runs, who owns it, and how risky it is. ## What is an AI system register? An AI system register is the full inventory of every AI system a company runs, regardless of how it got there. That includes a customer-facing feature, an internal copilot, or a marketing tool with a model switched on inside it that nobody called an AI project when they signed up. A working entry names what the system does, what data can reach it, which vendor or model sits behind it, who owns it, and a rough risk tier. Some call this same list an [AI register](/glossary/ai-register) rather than an AI system register. Most of the systems on it never started as a formal AI project, which is why the list has to go looking for them rather than wait to be told. ## Why does a security reviewer ask for it before anything else? A security or procurement reviewer asks one version of the same question first: what touches our data. Without a register, answering that means paging engineering, marketing, finance and support one by one, and hoping nobody forgot a tool. The [NIST AI RMF](/glossary/nist-ai-rmf) treats this as a named control, not a nice extra. Its Govern function includes a specific requirement: a mechanism to inventory AI systems, resourced according to how much risk the organisation is willing to carry. Everything a reviewer asks next, a data flow diagram, a vendor contract clause, an incident plan, gets scoped against rows already on this list. Skip the register, and the reviewer either stalls the process or signs off on a system nobody can fully describe. ## What should the register record? A register only earns its keep if a reviewer can answer their own questions from it, without a follow-up meeting. What follows is close to the version I hand a client: enough fields to answer a first review, and no field that exists only to look thorough. | What to record | Why a reviewer wants it | Who fills it in | | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Name the system and what it does. | A reviewer cannot scope a check against a system they cannot picture. | The system's product or engineering owner. | | Note whether it was built in-house or bought, and which vendor or model sits behind it. | A vendor's own controls become part of the risk the moment its API touches your data. | Whoever set up the account or the integration. | | List the data the system can see. | This sets the risk tier and decides which contract terms and legal duties actually apply. | The team that owns the data source, with legal signing off. | | Record who relies on the system's output. | Blast radius matters as much as data sensitivity when a reviewer decides how much scrutiny to apply. | The system owner, from usage or team headcount. | | Mark its deployment status: pilot, production or retired. | A pilot running on sample data is a different conversation from a live system holding real customer records. | The system owner, kept current as status changes. | | Name one internal owner. | A reviewer wants a person who can answer for the system, not a distribution list nobody reads. | Whoever runs the team that operates the system. | | Assign a risk tier. | This decides how much documentation, testing and sign-off the reviewer expects before anything ships. | Whoever runs the security or risk review, not the system's own owner. | | Log the date it was last checked. | A register that has not moved in a year gets treated the same as no register at all. | Whoever owns the register process, on a fixed schedule. | ## How do you build one in a week without buying a tool? None of this needs procurement. A spreadsheet, a shared document and five short conversations get a usable first version out the door. - **Monday.** Create the spreadsheet with those three columns, and seed it with every system already in use: the model inside the product, the support tool, the analytics dashboard that quietly added an AI summary. - **Tuesday and Wednesday.** Interview engineering, marketing, finance and support directly, not by survey. Ask each team what they actually use day to day, since a spreadsheet plug-in with a model behind it belongs on the list too. - **Thursday.** Fill in the vendor, data and risk-tier columns from what you heard, and flag anything nobody could describe clearly for a follow-up conversation rather than a guess. - **Friday.** Assign an owner to every row, pick a reviewer for the risk tiers, and put a recheck date on the calendar before anyone calls the list finished. ## What a register does not do Building the register is the easy part of this, and several harder parts of AI governance sit outside it. It does not replace a lawyer's read of a vendor contract. The register tells legal which vendor to check and what data reaches them. It says nothing about whether that vendor's specific contract terms are safe to sign, and those terms change often enough that last year's answer will not do. The registration duty in the [EU AI Act](/glossary/eu-ai-act) is a separate, public step for certain high-risk systems. It means registering under Article 49, in the database the Commission set up under Article 71, before the system goes live. An internal register is how you find out fast which systems might owe that separate duty; it is not a substitute for filing it. It does not stay accurate on its own, either. A register nobody owns drifts out of date within a quarter, and a stale register reads to a reviewer as no register at all. If you would rather someone else run the discovery and the first risk pass, an [AI Readiness & Risk Assessment](/services/ai-readiness-and-risk-assessment) does the same work in two weeks and hands you a finished register. The [starter kit](/resources/ai-governance-starter-kit) has a blank version of this table, ready to copy into your own document.

rows.text: An AI pilot never reached production because of an organisational gap, not a technical one. A demo only has to impress the person running it. Production has to survive a change of prompt, a change of model and a change of the person who built it, without anyone noticing except a number on a dashboard. Six conditions decide whether that gap closes. One named owner still answers for the system a year after launch, and a data classification signed off by someone with authority says what a vendor may see. An outcome number moves when the system works, matched by an eval that runs in the build pipeline before every release. Tracing shows which step produced a bad answer, and a rollback fires on a threshold, not an argument. Most stalled pilots are missing the first two, and the rest cannot be built until those exist.

rows.text: A pilot stalls in the space between working once and working every time. Most proof-of-concepts skip four things production always needs: a named owner who still answers a year after launch and a decision about which data may leave the building. They also lack a number that says whether the system is working, and an automatic check that catches a regression before a customer does. ## Where do pilots actually stop? ### Nobody owns the risk Pilots are usually built by whoever was curious enough to try. That person is rarely still around, or still in charge, once the project needs a decision about risk. Nobody has the standing to say the system is ready, and nobody has to explain a bad output to a customer or a regulator. Ownership is not a shared inbox or a Slack channel. It is one name attached to the outcome, with the budget and the authority to pause the system if it misbehaves. Without that name, every stall becomes permanent, because nobody is accountable for unsticking it. ### Legal has not said which data may leave Most pilots reach a vendor's API before anyone has classified the data going into the prompt. That is fine for a demo running on sample records. It stops a rollout the moment a security review asks what customer data the system touches and where it goes. The NIST AI RMF treats this as a governance decision under its Govern function, not a technical detail to settle after launch. Without a data classification written down in advance, every new use case reopens the same argument with legal. The pilot waits on a decision nobody has been asked to make yet. ### There is no measurable outcome A pilot that nobody can prove is working also cannot be proven to be failing, which is worse. Teams show accuracy on a curated test set, or a handful of good transcripts. Nobody has picked the business number the system is meant to move, such as tickets resolved, hours saved or the error rate on a defined task. Without that number, a debate about whether to invest further has no evidence on either side. The safest move for everyone involved is to let the pilot run quietly forever, rather than kill it or fund it properly. ### Nobody would notice a regression Prompts change, the underlying model changes on a provider's own schedule, and traffic drifts. Pilots rarely have a way to detect when any of that makes the output worse. There is no test suite running against real examples before a change ships, so a regression surfaces first as a customer complaint or a bad downstream decision, not as a failed build. That is the opposite of how the rest of the engineering organisation ships software. It is usually the reason a platform or security review declines to sign off. ## What has to be true to ship? Six conditions turn a pilot into something a platform team will actually run. None of them are exotic; most engineering teams already do the equivalent for every other production system they own. | Condition | What it means in practice | What its absence looks like | | ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | An owner. | One named person, on the team that runs the system, with authority to pause it. | No one can explain a bad output, so the stall becomes permanent. | | A data classification. | A written answer, agreed with whoever owns data risk, on what a vendor may store. | Every new use case reopens the same argument with legal. | | A measurable outcome. | One number the business already tracks, with a floor the system must clear. | Nobody can prove the pilot works, so it runs quietly forever instead of shipping or dying. | | Evals in CI. | Real test cases run on every prompt or model change; OWASP treats this as baseline hygiene. | A regression reaches a customer before anyone on the team sees it. | | Tracing and cost per outcome. | Every run logged well enough to reconstruct, with a cost a finance team can read. | Nobody can say what a run costs, or which step produced a bad answer. | | Rollback. | A rehearsed way to revert to the last prompt, model or version within minutes. | The team improvises during the first real incident instead of using a tested path. | For a system that touches decisions about people, the EU AI Act sets a similar bar for higher-risk uses. It requires a documented risk-management process, records that make a decision traceable and a human who can step in. Meeting the six conditions above gets most of the way there even for teams the Act does not yet cover. ## How would I sequence it? I run this as one pass, not six parallel workstreams, because the six conditions above depend on each other. You cannot set a rollback threshold before you have a measured outcome, and you cannot classify data before someone owns the decision to do it. ### Pick one process Choose a single workflow with enough volume to matter and an outcome you can measure without a survey, not five pilots running at once. An AI readiness and risk assessment is the fastest way to get that choice onto paper. Two weeks of reading the existing systems and vendor list end in a memo that names an owner candidate, a first data classification and the number the process should move. ### Build it in ninety days A 90-Day Production Sprint turns that memo into a running system. Evals get written alongside the first working version, rather than bolted on at the end. Tracing and cost per outcome go live on a dashboard from week one, and the rollback path gets rehearsed before real traffic arrives, not during the first incident. ### Hand it to someone who was in the room The internal owner should have written at least one eval case and watched the rollback rehearsal, so the runbook describes a system they already understand. A handover document given to someone who was not part of the build is a liability with a due date, not a transfer of knowledge. ## What this does not solve This sequence gets one process into production with the six conditions in place. Several harder governance questions stay outside it. Your risk appetite is still your call, not this sequence's. Two companies with the same pilot and the same data can reasonably choose different answers about what a vendor is allowed to see. That decision belongs to whoever owns risk at your company, not something a framework or an outside advisor can make for you. It does not replace a legal review of your contracts with model vendors. Classifying data tells your lawyers what question to ask; it does not answer whether a specific vendor's terms are acceptable, and that answer changes as vendors change their terms. The underlying model is exactly as reliable as it was before this sequence started. Evals catch regressions against the cases you thought to test. They do not catch every way a general-purpose model can fail on a case nobody wrote down, which is why the rollback path matters as much as the evals do. It does not scale to five processes at once. The sequence above is built for one workflow with one owner. Running it for a second or third process repeats the same ninety days; it does not shortcut them.

rows.text: ## What this is A CI workflow and an eval case format for one [agentic workflow](/glossary/agentic-workflow). The same discipline sits inside the [90-Day Production Sprint](/services/90-day-production-sprint). A prompt or model change should not merge without passing a test set first. ## The eval case format | Field | Purpose | Example | | -------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | | id | A stable name, so a failure is traceable across runs | refund-double-charge | | input | The exact prompt or tool call the agent receives | Customer says they were charged twice | | expected | A pass rule: an exact match, a check, or a second model acting as a grader | Refund issued, ticket closed, no invented apology | | tags | The failure mode a case guards against | prompt-injection, tool-misuse, refusal | ## The CI gate The workflow runs the eval set on every pull request, scores it, and blocks the merge under your floor. Nobody has to remember to run it by hand, which is the part that fails first once a team is busy. The tags borrow their shape from [OWASP's Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications](https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-for-large-language-model-applications/). Prompt injection and excessive agency (the agent doing something nobody asked it to) show up in a support agent as often as in a public chatbot. A tagged case catches the regression either way. ## What it is not It is not a considered eval set on its own. A handful of cases pulled from real conversations tests more than a long list invented at a desk. The starter takes no position on which cases you pick, and that part still maps to the MEASURE function (one of the framework's four functions) in [NIST's AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework).

rows.text: A pilot stalls in the space between working once and working every time. Most proof-of-concepts skip four things production always needs: a named owner who still answers a year after launch and a decision about which data may leave the building. They also lack a number that says whether the system is working, and an automatic check that catches a regression before a customer does.

rows.text: Pilots are usually built by whoever was curious enough to try. That person is rarely still around, or still in charge, once the project needs a decision about risk. Nobody has the standing to say the system is ready, and nobody has to explain a bad output to a customer or a regulator.

rows.text: Ownership is not a shared inbox or a Slack channel. It is one name attached to the outcome, with the budget and the authority to pause the system if it misbehaves. Without that name, every stall becomes permanent, because nobody is accountable for unsticking it.
